newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya opposition mulls disrupting state rally.
newsitem.headline: Kenya opposition mulls disrupting state rally.

text.p: Kenyan opposition and church leaders said they were considering disrupting a state occasion on Sunday to follow up a protest rally in Nairobi on Saturday that led to running battles with security forces.
Leaders said they might disrupt the annual Madaraka (Self Rule) Day rally to be addressed by President Daniel arap Moi at which Tanzania President Benjamin Mkapa is guest of honour.
"We want to give people a lot of whistles so that they can disrupt the meeting and then walk out," Reverend Timothy Njoya, a moderator in the Presbyterian Church of East Africa, told Reuters.
Opposition officials played down their plans for Sunday, saying they had had little time to plan coordinated action.

Police and paramilitary troops fought pitched battles with protesters on Saturday after they broke up a rally in central Uhuru (Freedom) Park called to press for constitutional reform but banned by the government.
At least two policemen were injured and many protesters were seriously beaten by police during more than six hours of unrest that brought central Nairobi to a standstill, eyewitnesses said.
London-based human rights group Amnesty International expressed grave concern over the violent break-up of the rally.

"The tear-gassing and beatings meted out to peaceful protesters was unwarranted and excessive, particularly since the law under which the government declared the meeting illegal contravenes international human rights standards which Kenya has ratified," an Amnesty spokesman said.
At least three opposition activists were arrested but later released by police, David Kabeberi, adviser to opposition FORD-Asili leader Kenneth Matiba, told Reuters. There was no government comment.
Nairobi's central business district was deserted on Saturday night.
At least three cars were set on fire, dozens of shops were looted, stalls were burned and cars stoned as the riot spread downtown from the Kenyatta Avenue district in Saturday's rioting.
Police and General Service Unit paramilitary troops fired live rounds and teargas grenades and wielded clubs to quell the protest.
Crowds targeted shops and cars owned by ethnic Asians from the Indian sub-continent, according to eyewitnesses.
Opposition MP Raila Odinga and other opposition leaders told reporters on Saturday they planned to return to Uhuru Park.
Opposition activists compared the rally and riot to protests in the years before the first democratic elections in 1992, won by the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU).
"In 1992 the situation was not as bad as it is now. Now people have a lot more resolve because they have a lot less to lose," said Robert Shaw, a supporter of the unregistered Safina party.
"The broad alliance of opposition parties, NGO's (non-governmental organisations) and churches shows that this is not going to go away. This is going to gather momentum," he said.
The National Convention Assembly (NCA), an umbrella for church leaders and opposition parties, had called the rally to press for a minimum package of constitutional reform.
Diplomats, human rights groups and opposition politicians accuse the government of deploying the Public Order Act on behalf of KANU.
President Moi must call presidential and parliamentary elections by the end of the year, pitting KANU against an opposition divided along ethnic, political and personal lines.
The NCA argues fair multi-party elections are impossible when Kenya retains a constitution designed for a one-party state. It proposes a referendum to ascertain popular support for reform.
An aide to leading opposition politician, Kenneth Matiba, said his boss was meeting other opposition figures at a hideout in the city to plan their next move.

Matiba, a leading proponent of constitutional change, told Reuters through Kabeberi: "We will make the city hell for Moi and his cronies. I will not sleep tonight because I have to be with the people and this means Moi cannot sleep either because his security will have to keep on briefing him."
